mainTopic: Fire damage: who is responsible, what the Torah's fire פסוק covers, and an אגדה about disaster and the righteous
overview: The עמוד opens by finishing רבי יוחנן's statement from the previous עמוד: someone who hands fire to a חרש, שוטה וקטן is liable only if the fire was already set up to spread. רב נחמן בר יצחק then says the משנה's word for fanning a fire may be read either ליבה or ניבה, and he backs up each reading with a פסוק. A ברייתא teaches that someone who fans a fire along with the wind is liable only if his own fanning was strong enough to spread it alone. The גמרא challenges this from winnowing on שבת and gets four answers, ending with רב אשי: שבת looks at planned work, but in damages this is only גרמא, which is exempt. A new משנה rules that one who sends a fire pays even for burned wood, stones or earth. רבא then explains why the פסוק names thorns, a grain stack, standing grain and a field. Along the way, רבי יהודה and the רבנן each learn different rules from the words קמה and או. The עמוד closes with an אגדה: disaster comes because of the wicked but strikes the righteous first, and אביי comforts רב יוסף by explaining that this is a kindness to the righteous.

steps.title: When the sender's own act surely caused the fire
steps.stepSummary: This line ends a statement from the previous עמוד. The sender is liable once he handed over thin wood chips and a candle, because then his own act clearly caused the fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: [He is not liable until he gave over] thin wood chips and a candle, because in that case his own action definitely caused the fire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבי יוחנן's statement that started on the previous עמוד. In his view, the sender becomes liable only when he hands over a fire that is already set up to spread, like wood chips and a candle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the sender only hands over a coal or a small flame, it is the חרש's handling that turns it into a real fire, so the sender is exempt. If he hands over chips and a candle, the fire is basically ready to go. Then the damage is clearly his doing.

keyTerms.meaning: Thin wood chips or kindling that catch fire easily

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, a sender is liable through a חרש, שוטה וקטן only when he handed over a fire so ready to spread that his own act clearly caused the damage.

phrases.english: thin wood chips, a candle,
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from the previous עמוד: he is liable only once he handed over these things.

phrases.english: since in that case his own action definitely caused it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a statement that began on the previous עמוד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יוחנן, the sender is liable only when he handed over a fire ready to spread, such as chips and a candle, so that his own action clearly caused the damage.

steps.title: Two valid ways to read the word in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about sending fire through a competent person. רב נחמן בר יצחק says the word in the משנה may be read either ליבה or ניבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: If he sent the fire with a competent person, the competent person is liable, etc. רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Whoever reads it 'ליבה' is not wrong, and whoever reads it 'ניבה' is not wrong.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה. רב נחמן בר יצחק comments on how one of its words should be read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה goes on to say that if someone else came and fanned the flame, he is liable. There were two ways of reading that word: ליבה ('fanned') and ניבה ('blew'). רב נחמן בר יצחק says neither reading is a mistake, and both describe someone making the fire bigger.
steps.confusionAlert: רב נחמן בר יצחק is not arguing about the law here. Both readings describe the same act of making the fire grow; he is only discussing the wording.

phrases.english: If he sent it in the hand of a competent person –
the competent person is liable, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' points to the next part of the משנה: if someone else fanned the fire, the one who fanned is liable. That's what is being discussed.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
Whoever reads 'libba' (fanned) is not mistaken,
and whoever reads 'nibba' (blew) is not mistaken.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new phrase in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both readings of the משנה, ליבה and ניבה, are acceptable.

steps.title: פסוקים supporting both readings
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק backs each reading with a פסוק. ליבה is like לבת אש ('a flame of fire'), and ניבה is like ניב שפתים ('the utterance of the lips').
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever reads 'ליבה' is not mistaken, as it is written: 'In a flame (לבת) of fire.' And whoever reads 'ניבה' is not mistaken, as it is written: 'He creates the ניב of the lips.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק proves from פסוקים that both words fit the case of someone making a fire grow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ליבה comes from לבה, a flame, so it means making the fire flare up. ניבה connects to ניב שפתים, the breath coming out of the lips, so it means blowing on the fire. Each word has a source in תנ״ך, so neither reading is wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (introduces a פסוק)
The utterance or breath of the lips

phrases.english: Whoever reads 'libba' is not mistaken –
as it is written: 'In a flame of fire.'
and whoever reads 'nibba' is not mistaken –
as it is written: 'He creates the utterance of the lips.'
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 57:19. The idea is the breath coming from the lips, like blowing on a fire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for each reading named in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: That both ליבה and ניבה are correct readings of the משנה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 3:2, 'בלבת אש', and ישעיהו 57:19, 'בורא ניב שפתים'.

steps.title: The משנה: when the wind fans, all are exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that if the wind fanned the fire, everyone involved is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: If the wind fanned it, they are all exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה. This sets up the ברייתא that comes right after and explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the wind is what spread the fire, the damage is not blamed on any of the people involved. This raises a question: what if a person was fanning at the same time as the wind? The next step answers that.

phrases.english: If the wind fanned it –
they are all exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the wind spreads the fire, none of the people involved are liable.

steps.title: ברייתא: a person fanning together with the wind
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if a person fanned the fire while the wind also fanned it, he is liable only if his own fanning was strong enough to spread the fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If he fanned it and the wind also fanned it, then if his fanning was enough to make it flare up, he is liable; and if not, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that spells out the משנה's rule about the wind for the case where a person and the wind fan at the same time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deciding question is whether the person's fanning could have spread the fire alone. If it could, the fire would have spread even without the wind, so he is liable. If not, the wind is the real cause, and he is exempt like everyone in the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: Enough to make it flare up

steps.whatToRemember: A person who fans along with the wind is liable only if his own fanning would have been enough to spread the fire.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a clear test for shared causes of damage: a person is liable only when his own act was strong enough to cause the damage alone.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
If he fanned it and the wind fanned it,

phrases.aramaic: אִם יֵשׁ בְּלִבּוּיוֹ כְּדֵי לְלַבּוֹתָהּ – חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: if his fanning had enough to fan it – he is liable,
and if not – he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the משנה's rule from step 4 for the case where a person and the wind fan together.
steps.raayaObject: How far the משנה's exemption goes when the wind fans the fire.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: he is liable only if his own fanning was enough to spread the fire.

steps.title: Why not treat him like someone winnowing with the wind's help?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. On שבת, one who winnows with the wind's help is liable, so why is the fanner exempt here?
steps.simpleTranslation: Why is he exempt? Let him be like a person who winnows on שבת while the wind helps him, who is liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the ברייתא from Step 5, which exempted a person whose fanning was not strong enough to spread the fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On שבת, a person who tosses grain into the air is liable for winnowing, even though the wind does part of the work. So partial human effort plus wind counts as his act. The גמרא asks why fanning a fire together with the wind should be any different.

keyTerms.meaning: One who winnows: tossing grain into the air so the wind separates the chaff

phrases.english: Why?
phrases.notes: He means: why is the person who fanned exempt when his fanning was not enough by itself?

phrases.english: Let it be like one who winnows while the wind helps him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the exemption in the ברייתא of Step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's exemption of one whose fanning was not enough to spread the fire
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: On שבת, human effort plus wind counts as the person's act (winnowing), so the same should apply to fanning a fire

steps.title: אביי: he fanned from one side and the wind from the other
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the person fanned from one side and the wind blew from the other side, so his fanning did not help.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: What case are we dealing with here? A case where he fanned from one side and the wind fanned it from a different side.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge. He explains the ברייתא is talking about a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With winnowing, the person and the wind work together in the same direction. In אביי's case they work from opposite sides, and the fire went where the wind pushed it. So the person did not help spread the fire at all.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a ruling to a specific case)

phrases.english: אביי said:
What case are we dealing with here?
A case where he fanned from one side,
and the wind fanned it from a different side.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 6 by narrowing the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The person and the wind worked together, like winnowing
steps.terutzMaskana: They worked from opposite sides, so the person added nothing to the spread

steps.title: רבא: an unusual wind came and spread the fire
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the person fanned in a normal wind, and then an unusual, unexpected wind spread the fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A case where he fanned in a normal wind, and then an unusual wind came and fanned it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different answer to the same challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person's fanning in a normal wind was not enough to spread the fire. The fire spread only because of an unusual wind that he could not have expected. So the spread is not blamed on him.

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא אָמַר: כְּגוֹן שֶׁלִּיבָּה בְּרוּחַ מְצוּיָה,
phrases.english: רבא said: A case where he fanned it in a normal wind,
and the wind fanned it with an unusual wind.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: כְּגוֹן שֶׁלִּיבָּה בְּרוּחַ מְצוּיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to Step 6, different from אביי's
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The wind that helped was an ordinary wind, like in winnowing
steps.terutzMaskana: An unexpected wind did the spreading, so the person is not responsible

steps.title: רבי זירא: he only blew lightly on it
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא explains that the person only warmed the fire with his breath and did not really fan it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: A case where he only blew on it lightly with his breath.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא gives a third answer to the same challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the person's act was tiny, just breathing on the fire. That is too weak to count as real fanning, so the spread is credited to the wind and not to him.

keyTerms.meaning: He blew on it lightly with his breath

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר: כְּגוֹן דְּצַמְּרַהּ צַמּוֹרֵי.
phrases.english: רבי זירא said: A case where he blew on it lightly with his breath.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר: כְּגוֹן דְּצַמְּרַהּ צַמּוֹרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to Step 6
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He fanned the fire properly together with the wind
steps.terutzMaskana: His act was only light blowing, too weak to count

steps.title: רב אשי: שבת and damages work differently
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the comparison to winnowing does not apply. שבת cares about planned work, but in damages this is only indirect causing, and that is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: When we say that one who winnows with the wind's help is liable, that is only for שבת, because the Torah forbade planned, purposeful work. But here it is only indirect causing, and one who causes damage indirectly is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers in a completely different way. He does not narrow the case. Instead, he says the rule from שבת cannot be applied to damages at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On שבת, what counts is that the person's planned goal was achieved, even with the wind's help. In נזקין we ask who directly did the damage. When the wind finishes the job, the person is only a גרמא, an indirect cause, and גרמא בנזקין פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: Planned, purposeful work, which is the kind of work forbidden on שבת
One who causes damage indirectly is exempt

steps.whatToRemember: Four answers for why the fanner is exempt: אביי (opposite sides), רבא (unusual wind), רבי זירא (only light breath), רב אשי (שבת counts planned work, but in damages this is only גרמא, which is exempt).
steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי does not disagree with the rule about winnowing on שבת. He agrees the winnower is liable on שבת. He only says that rule does not carry over to damages.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a key principle: the same physical act can count as 'your act' for שבת and still be only indirect causing for damages.

phrases.english: רב אשי said:
When we say that one who winnows while the wind helps him is liable,
that applies only to the laws of שבת,
because the Torah forbade planned, purposeful work;
but here, it is merely indirect causing,
and indirect causing in damages is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: כִּי אָמְרִינַן זוֹרֶה וְרוּחַ מְסַיַּיעְתּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fourth answer to Step 6. It rejects the comparison itself instead of narrowing the case
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between areas of law (שבת versus נזקין)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule from winnowing on שבת should apply to damages too
steps.terutzMaskana: שבת follows מלאכת מחשבת, but damages caused partly by the wind are only גרמא, which is exempt

steps.title: New משנה: a fire that burns wood, stones or earth
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that one who sends a fire is liable even if it burns wood, stones or earth.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who sends out a fire, and it burns wood, stones or earth, is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches that the one who sent the fire is liable even when the fire damaged things like stones and earth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the topic was who is responsible for spreading a fire. Now the משנה asks what kinds of damage he pays for. The answer is that he pays even for damage to stones and to the ground itself, not only for crops.

keyTerms.meaning: One who sends out a fire
Earth, the soil of the field

phrases.english: משנה:
One who sends out a fire,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָכְלָה עֵצִים אוֹ אֲבָנִים אוֹ עָפָר – חַיָּיב;
phrases.english: and it burned wood, or stones, or earth, is liable;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of fanning ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who sends a fire is liable even if it burns wood, stones or earth

steps.title: The פסוק behind the משנה's rule
steps.stepSummary: The משנה brings a פסוק that lists the field itself among the things the fire burns, and says the one who lit it must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'If a fire goes out and finds thorns, and a stack of grain, or standing grain, or the field is burned, the one who lit the fire must pay.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה backs up its rule with a פסוק from the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists 'the field' (השדה) among the things the fire burns. That shows the person pays even when the ground itself is damaged, and not only for crops. This supports liability for things like earth and stones.

keyTerms.meaning: Grain still standing in the field
The one who lit the fire

phrases.english: As it says: 'If a fire goes out and finds thorns,

phrases.aramaic: וְנֶאֱכַל גָּדִישׁ אוֹ הַקָּמָה אוֹ הַשָּׂדֶה,
phrases.english: and a stack of grain, or standing grain, or the field is consumed,
the one who lit the fire must surely pay.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the ruling in Step 11
steps.raayaObject: Liability for fire damage to wood, stones and earth
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 22:5, which lists 'the field' among the things damaged

steps.title: Why does the Torah list four things the fire burns?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks why the פסוק needs to name thorns, a grain stack, standing grain and a field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Why did the Torah need to write 'thorns,' 'a stack of grain,' 'standing grain' and 'field'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא on the new משנה begins with a question from רבא. He asks why the פסוק about fire names so many different things. This sets up the explanations that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah does not waste words. If one example could teach the law of fire damage, the other three look extra, so each one must teach something of its own.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Merciful One', a name for ה׳, used when saying what the Torah wrote
Standing grain, still growing in the field
'Why do I need it?', a question asking what a word adds

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rava said:
Why do I need that the Merciful One wrote
phrases.notes: He is asking about the פסוק the משנה just quoted, שמות 22:5.

phrases.english: 'thorns,' 'a stack of grain,' 'standing grain' and 'field'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the wording of the פסוק that the משנה quoted in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What each of the four items in the פסוק adds.

steps.title: Thorns and a grain stack each teach something new
steps.stepSummary: Both are needed. From thorns alone we would exempt a grain stack, and from a grain stack alone we would exempt thorns.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both are needed. If the Torah wrote only 'thorns,' I would think the Torah makes him liable only for thorns, because fire is often near them and people are often careless. But a grain stack is not usually near fire and people are not usually careless with it, so I would say he is not liable. And if the Torah wrote only 'grain stack,' I would think he is liable only for it, because it is a big loss. But thorns are a small loss, so I would say he is not liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers part of רבא's question. It shows that thorns and a grain stack are both needed, because each one has a reason that the other one lacks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Thorns have the 'easy to be liable' reason: fire is often near them, so carelessness is common. A grain stack has a different reason: losing it is costly. Neither reason carries over to the other item, so the Torah has to say both.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They are needed', meaning each word teaches something the others don't
'I would have said', the mistaken idea we would have had
A big loss / a small loss

steps.confusionAlert: This answer only explains thorns and the grain stack. The גמרא deals with קמה separately in the next steps.

phrases.english: They are needed; for if the Merciful One had written only 'thorns,'
I would have said:
it is thorns for which the Merciful One makes him liable,
because fire is commonly near them,
and it is common that one is careless;
but a stack of grain,
where fire is not commonly near it,
and it is not common that one is careless, I would say he is not liable.
And if the Merciful One had written only 'a stack of grain,'
I would have said:
for a grain stack the Merciful One makes him liable,
because it is a big loss;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל קוֹצִים – דְּהֶפְסֵד מוּעָט, אֵימָא לָא.
phrases.english: but thorns, which are a small loss, I would say he is not liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's question as it applies to thorns and the grain stack.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each item has its own reason for liability that would not carry over to the other, so both must be written.

steps.title: What does the word 'standing grain' add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the Torah also needs to write קמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need 'standing grain'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks about the third word, קמה. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Thorns and a grain stack were already explained. So קמה needs its own reason for being in the פסוק.

phrases.english: Why do I need 'standing grain'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from thorns and grain stack to the next word in the list.

steps.title: Standing grain teaches: only things out in the open
steps.stepSummary: Just as standing grain is out in the open, the fire law covers only things that are out in the open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as standing grain is out in the open, so too, one is liable only for things that are out in the open.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that קמה teaches a limit. A person who lights a fire pays only for things that were out in the open, not for hidden things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Standing grain is easy to see in the field. The גמרא uses it as a model: only things like it, out in the open, are covered. Hidden things (טמון) are left out.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Just as ... so too', a way of learning a rule from an example

phrases.aramaic: מָה קָמָה בְּגָלוּי – אַף כֹּל בְּגָלוּי.
phrases.english: Just as standing grain is in the open, so too everything must be in the open.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about קמה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: קמה limits fire liability to things that are out in the open.

steps.title: What does 'standing grain' teach for רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה makes a person pay even for hidden things, so the limit from קמה cannot be his reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי יהודה, who makes a person liable for hidden things damaged by fire, why do I need 'standing grain'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer. רבי יהודה holds that a person pays even for hidden things, so for him קמה cannot mean 'only things in the open.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 16 works only for those who exempt hidden things. רבי יהודה disagrees with that rule, so he must use the word קמה for something else.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who holds one pays even for hidden things burned by fire

phrases.english: And according to Rabbi Yehuda, who makes him liable
for damage by fire to hidden things,
why do I need 'standing grain'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה דִּמְחַיֵּיב אַנִּזְקֵי טָמוּן בָּאֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether step 16's answer works for every opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of קמה in step 16 to exclude hidden things.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה does not exempt hidden things, so the word must teach him something else.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the word קמה teaches according to רבי יהודה, who makes one pay even for hidden things.

steps.title: For רבי יהודה: it includes everything that stands tall
steps.stepSummary: For רבי יהודה, קמה includes all things that have height, not just crops.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include everything that has height.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that for רבי יהודה, קמה teaches that anything standing tall is included in the fire law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Standing grain stands upright. So for רבי יהודה the word shows that anything that stands tall is covered, not just grain. This is a different lesson from the 'out in the open' one.

keyTerms.meaning: To include, to add more cases
Things that have height, that stand tall

phrases.english: To include all things that have height.
phrases.notes: קמה (standing grain) and קומה (height) sound alike, which is why the word points to tall things.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by giving רבי יהודה a different lesson from קמה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the word a different lesson for this opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: For רבי יהודה, the word קמה would have nothing to teach.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי יהודה, קמה includes everything that stands tall.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: For רבי יהודה, קמה includes everything that stands tall.

steps.title: Where do the רבנן learn about things that stand tall?
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן already used קמה for 'out in the open', so where do they learn that tall things are included?
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, where do they learn that everything that has height is included?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the רבנן. They used קמה for the 'out in the open' rule, so they still need a source for including tall things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One word usually cannot teach two separate lessons. Since the רבנן used קמה for the hidden-things rule, the גמרא asks what source they have for the 'tall things' rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, who disagree with רבי יהודה and exempt hidden things
'From where do they know it?', asking for a source

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, to include all things that have height,
from where do they learn it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן, לְרַבּוֹת כׇּל בַּעֲלֵי קוֹמָה מְנָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the lesson from step 18 back on the רבנן.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's source for including things that stand tall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רבנן already used קמה for the 'out in the open' rule, so they need another source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The רבנן's source for including things that stand tall.

steps.title: The רבנן learn it from the word 'או'
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn that tall things are included from the extra word 'or' in 'או הקמה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: They learn it from 'or the standing grain.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן get the rule about tall things from the word 'או' ('or') that comes before קמה in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'או' is treated as adding more cases. So the רבנן get both rules: 'out in the open' from קמה, and 'all tall things' from 'או'.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Or', here treated as a word that includes more cases

steps.whatToRemember: קמה teaches two possible lessons. The רבנן learn 'only things out in the open' from קמה and 'all tall things' from 'או'. רבי יהודה, who makes one pay even for hidden things, learns 'all tall things' from קמה itself.

phrases.english: They derive it from 'or the standing grain.'
phrases.notes: The extra word 'או' is what adds more cases.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the רבנן's source, which raises the next question: what does רבי יהודה do with the word או (step 21).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finds a different word in the פסוק as the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן would have no source for including tall things.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן learn it from the word 'או'.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both opinions include tall things. Only the source differs: קמה for רבי יהודה, 'או' for the רבנן.

steps.title: רבי יהודה uses 'or' to make each item count separately
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה does not need אוֹ to include tall things, so he uses it for לחלק: each item is its own case of liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה? He needs the word 'or' to divide the items.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן used the extra אוֹ to include tall things. The גמרא now explains what רבי יהודה does with that אוֹ, since he already learned 'tall things' from קמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, the word אוֹ teaches that you pay for burning any one of the listed items. The fire does not have to burn all of them together. So the same word does a different job in his reading.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Or': here, the extra word in the פסוק
He needs it for (a different teaching)
To divide: each item counts on its own

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda?
phrases.notes: The question is left unsaid: what does רבי יהודה do with the extra 'or'?

phrases.english: He needs 'or' to divide.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how רבי יהודה uses the word that the רבנן used in step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: For רבי יהודה, אוֹ teaches לחלק: liability for each item separately.

steps.title: Where do the Rabbis learn that each item counts separately?
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן used אוֹ for tall things, so the גמרא asks where they learn לחלק.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן: from where do they learn 'to divide'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where the רבנן get the rule that each item counts on its own. They already used the word אוֹ for something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that you pay even if only one item burns. Since the רבנן spent אוֹ on including tall things, they need another source for this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do they know it?

phrases.english: And the Rabbis: 'to divide', from where do they have it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the question of step 21 back onto the רבנן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source the רבנן use for לחלק.

steps.title: The Rabbis learn it from 'or the field'
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn לחלק from the second אוֹ, in אוֹ הַשָּׂדֶה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They derive it from 'or the field'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק has a second אוֹ, before 'the field'. The רבנן learn לחלק from that one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two 'or's in the פסוק. The רבנן use the first for tall things and the second for לחלק, so both rules are covered.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Or the field': the second 'or' in the פסוק

phrases.english: They derive it from 'or the field'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן learn לחלק from the אוֹ in אוֹ הַשָּׂדֶה.

steps.title: For רבי יהודה, the second 'or' just matches the wording
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה learns nothing from אוֹ הַשָּׂדֶה. The Torah wrote it only to match אוֹ הַקָּמָה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה? Since the Torah wrote 'or the standing grain', it also wrote 'or the field'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what רבי יהודה does with the second אוֹ. His answer is that it teaches nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה already got לחלק from the first אוֹ. So the second אוֹ is there only so the list reads smoothly, and no new הלכה comes from it.

keyTerms.meaning: Since (it wrote one thing, it also wrote the other)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think every extra word must teach something for everyone. Here רבי יהודה says this word is only for style.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda?
phrases.notes: Again the question is left unsaid: what does he do with 'or the field'?

phrases.english: Since the Merciful One wrote 'or the standing grain',
He wrote 'or the field'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the matching question for רבי יהודה about the second אוֹ.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי יהודה, the second אוֹ only matches the first.

steps.title: Why does the verse need the word 'field'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word שָׂדֶה itself adds.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need 'field'?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא moves from the word אוֹ to the word שָׂדֶה, and asks what it teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק already lists stacked grain and standing grain. The גמרא wants to know what the word 'field' adds on top of those.

phrases.english: 'Field': why do I need it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to a new word in the same פסוק.

steps.title: 'Field' includes scorching a plowed field
steps.stepSummary: שָׂדֶה makes you liable when fire licks a plowed field and scorches its stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: To include a case where the fire licked his plowed field and scorched its stones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'field' adds damage to the land itself. An example is fire that burns over a plowed field and scorches the stones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here nothing standing on the land burns. The land itself is harmed, and it has to be plowed again. The word שָׂדֶה makes this damage count.

phrases.english: To include where it licked his plowed field
And scorched its stones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שָׂדֶה includes damage to a plowed field and its stones.

steps.title: Then the Torah should have written only 'field'
steps.stepSummary: If you pay even for a scorched field, you surely pay for things that burn up completely. So why list the others?
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the Torah write only 'field', and it would not need those others!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer. If 'field' covers even light damage, the other items seem obvious and unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A scorched field is only partly damaged. Stacked or standing grain burns up completely. So if you pay for the field, the other words look extra.

phrases.english: Let the Merciful One write 'field',
And it would not need those!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks step 26 by making the other words look unneeded.
steps.kashyaTarget: Why the Torah lists גדיש and קמה at all.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If light damage to the field counts, total damage to other things should obviously count too.

steps.title: Without the other words, we would limit it to the field
steps.stepSummary: With only שָׂדֶה, we would think the law covers just what is in a field. The other words teach that it covers anything.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed. If the Torah wrote only 'field', I would say: what is in the field, yes; anything else, no. So it teaches us.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the other words are needed. 'Field' alone could be read as limiting the law to field items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry here is a narrow reading, not a weaker case. If the Torah wrote only שָׂדֶה, you might pay only for field-type things. The full list shows the fire law covers all property.
steps.whatToRemember: Each word in the fire פסוק has a job. אוֹ (one or both) handles לחלק and tall things. שָׂדֶה adds damage to the land. The full list shows the law is not limited to field items.

phrases.english: It is needed;
For if the Merciful One had written 'field',
I would have said:
What is in the field, yes,
Anything else, no;
So it teaches us.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכא: each word blocks a mistaken narrow reading.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only שָׂדֶה, liability would cover only field items.
steps.terutzMaskana: The list teaches liability for any property the fire damages.

steps.title: Disaster comes because of the wicked but starts with the righteous
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני, quoting רבי יונתן: פורענות comes only when רשעים are in the world, and it starts with the צדיקים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: disaster comes to the world only when there are wicked people in the world, and it begins only with the righteous first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from הלכה to an אגדה based on the same fire פסוק. This step states the idea, and the next steps give the proofs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate claims. The cause of disaster is the presence of the wicked. Even so, the first ones hurt are the righteous.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said
That Rabbi Yonatan said:
Disaster does not come to the world
Except when the wicked are in the world,
And it does not begin
Except with the righteous first,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the legal discussion for an אגדה on the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Disaster comes because of the wicked but begins with the righteous.

steps.title: Fire goes out only when there are thorns
steps.stepSummary: 'If a fire goes out and finds thorns': the fire (disaster) comes when thorns (the wicked) are there.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'If a fire goes out and finds thorns.' When does fire go out? When there are thorns for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the first claim. In the פסוק, the thorns stand for the wicked, and the fire stands for disaster.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fire spreads because it finds thorns to catch on. In the same way, disaster comes because wicked people are there.

phrases.english: As it is said: 'If a fire goes out and finds thorns';
When does fire go out?
When thorns are there for it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the first half of step 29.
steps.raayaObject: Disaster comes only when the wicked are present.

steps.title: 'The stack was consumed': the righteous are hit first
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says וְנֶאֱכַל (was consumed), not וְאָכַל (consumed). This shows the stack (the righteous) was already burned first.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it begins with the righteous first, as it says 'and a stack was consumed.' It does not say 'and it consumed a stack', but 'and a stack was consumed': the stack was already consumed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the second claim from the exact wording of the פסוק. The stack of grain stands for the righteous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The passive form וְנֶאֱכַל suggests something that already happened. So the stack, meaning the righteous, was burned before the fire reached the thorns.
steps.whatToRemember: Through the fire פסוק, רבי יונתן teaches that the wicked bring disaster, but the righteous suffer from it first.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵינָהּ מַתְחֶלֶת אֶלָּא מִן הַצַּדִּיקִים תְּחִלָּה,
phrases.english: And it begins only with the righteous first,
As it is said: 'And a stack was consumed';
'And it consumed a stack' is not said,
Rather 'and a stack was consumed':
That the stack was already consumed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the second half of step 29.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The passive wording וְנֶאֱכַל גָּדִישׁ in שמות 22:5.

steps.title: The destroyer does not tell righteous from wicked
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף teaches a ברייתא explaining why the Jews could not leave their houses on the night of מכת בכורות. Once the משחית is let loose, it does not separate righteous from wicked.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף taught: Why does the פסוק say 'None of you shall go out of the door of his house until morning'? Because once the destroyer is given permission, it does not tell the difference between righteous and wicked people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from רב יוסף that supports the idea that disaster hits the righteous too. He uses the command to stay indoors on the night of מכת בכורות as his source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plague was only meant for the Egyptians, so why did the Jews have to stay inside? The ברייתא answers that once the משחית is unleashed, it hits whoever is in its path, good or bad. Staying indoors was their protection.

keyTerms.meaning: He taught (a ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה)
The destroyer, the force sent to bring the plague

phrases.english: Rav Yosef taught:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"And none of you shall go out,
phrases.notes: שמות 12:22. This was said about the night of מכת בכורות.

phrases.english: from the opening of his house until morning"?
Once permission is given to the destroyer,
it does not distinguish between the righteous and the wicked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second teaching that supports the theme of step 29, that disaster reaches the righteous too.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once the משחית has permission, it strikes without telling righteous from wicked.

steps.title: It even starts with the righteous
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא goes further: the destroyer actually begins with the righteous. The proof is a פסוק in יחזקאל that lists צדיק before רשע.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that, it begins with the righteous first, as it says: 'And I will cut off from you the righteous and the wicked.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a stronger claim, that the righteous are hit first, and proves it from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from the word order: the פסוק says 'צדיק ורשע,' putting the righteous first. This matches what רבי יונתן said in step 29, that disaster starts with the צדיקים.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but even more

phrases.english: And not only that, but
it begins with the righteous first,
as it is said:
"And I will cut off from you the righteous and the wicked."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא עוֹד, אֶלָּא שֶׁמַּתְחִיל מִן הַצַּדִּיקִים תְּחִלָּה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the claim of step 32 one step further and backs it with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the destroyer starts with the righteous
steps.raayaSupportSource: יחזקאל 21:8, where צדיק is listed before רשע

steps.title: רב יוסף cries over the fate of the righteous
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף weeps: are even all these righteous people treated as if they were nothing?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף cried and said: Are all these righteous people also counted as nothing?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף is upset by the teaching he just taught. He cries out that it seems unfair for the righteous to be treated as worthless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a technical question but an emotional challenge. If the righteous die along with the wicked, and even first, it looks like their goodness counts for nothing. This sets up אביי's answer.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef cried:
Are all these, too,
phrases.notes: He means all these righteous people.

phrases.english: compared to nothing?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts with pain to the teaching that the righteous are struck first.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea in step 33 that disaster starts with the righteous
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the righteous are struck first, it seems their righteousness is worth nothing, which feels unjust.

steps.title: אביי: being taken first is a kindness
steps.stepSummary: אביי comforts רב יוסף: dying first is actually good for the righteous, because they are taken away before the evil comes.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: It is a kindness for them, as it says: 'For the righteous one is taken away because of the evil to come.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers רב יוסף's pain by showing that the righteous dying first is a favor to them, and he brings a פסוק to prove it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף saw early death as a sign the righteous don't matter. אביי flips it: the צדיק is gathered in early so he will not have to suffer through the coming disaster. The פסוק in ישעיהו supports this.

keyTerms.meaning: Is gathered in, taken away (passes away)

steps.whatToRemember: Disaster can strike the righteous first, but אביי teaches that this is a kindness: they are spared from seeing and suffering the evil that follows.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
It is a kindness for them,
as it is written:
"For because of the evil, the righteous one is taken away."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: טֵיבוּתָא הוּא לְגַבַּיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's cry from step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: what looks like a punishment is really a kindness
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The righteous dying first shows they are treated as worthless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The righteous are taken first as a kindness, so they are spared the coming suffering.

steps.title: Opening a new teaching from רב יהודה in the name of רב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces a new statement of רב יהודה quoting רב. The statement itself comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup: the גמרא is getting ready to bring a new teaching. The actual words of the teaching come right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the names are given here, so nothing has been taught yet. Keep in mind who is speaking, because the next line will be their statement.

keyTerms.meaning: רב יהודה said that רב said (a common way of quoting a teacher)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda says that Rav says:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching after אביי's answer closes the previous discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduction only; the content of the statement follows in the next lines.
